claims.text: Adding a small fraction of Ag to the Cu phase of a W–Cu composite will increase the composite thermal conductivity.
Ag addition will retain the mechanical durability of the W–Cu composite.
Ag addition will retain the irradiation resistance of the W–Cu composite.
A typical binary W–Cu composite contains W particles dispersed in a Cu matrix and approximately 30–70 vol% W.
The proposed intervention is to add 1–3 wt% Ag to the Cu matrix.
The added Ag should be homogeneously distributed without forming separate phases.
Ag atoms substitute into the Cu lattice.
Substitutional Ag reduces electron scattering at grain boundaries and interfaces.
Ag addition does not significantly alter the W–Cu interface or composite microstructure.
Ag increases the electrical conductivity of the Cu phase through improved electron mobility.
The increased electrical conductivity of the Cu phase produces increased thermal conductivity.
Ag does not embrittle the composite because it has an atomic size similar to Cu.
Ag does not degrade irradiation resistance because it has low neutron activation.
The W–Cu–Ag composite will have 5–15% higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable binary W–Cu composite.
The mechanical strength of the W–Cu–Ag composite will remain at least 95% of the binary baseline.
The irradiation resistance of the W–Cu–Ag composite will remain at least 95% of the binary baseline.
The predicted effects hold only for homogeneous Ag additions below 3 wt% and application temperatures below 500°C.
Excessive or inhomogeneously distributed Ag may degrade composite properties.
No direct evidence is available for Ag addition in W–Cu composites.
The hypothesis is extrapolated from Ag effects in Cu alloys and general ternary-alloying behavior.

contradictions.description: The intervention permits 1–3 wt% Ag, including 3 wt%, whereas the stated validity boundary requires Ag to be below 3 wt%.
The conditions allow temperatures up to approximately 500°C, while the boundary requires temperatures below 500°C, making applicability at 500°C inconsistent.
